title.en: Rising administrative recognition of autism across health and education systems in Chile, 2019–2025: a national multisource surveillance study

manuscript.html: Rising administrative recognition of autism across health and education systems in Chile, 2019–2025: a national multisource surveillance study
Amaru Agüero Jiménez; Patricia Soto Icaza
Centro de Investigación en Complejidad Social, Facultad de Gobierno, Universidad del Desarrollo
Correspondence to: Patricia Soto Icaza, patriciasoto@udd.cl (affiliation above). [Postal address and telephone to be completed.]
Summary

Background. Autism counts in routine records are rising while coverage, coding and definitions change together. We examined recording across Chile's public health and education systems, 2019–2025, and whether growth survived fixed institutional participation and case definitions.

Methods. National multisource study of unlinked routine records: public hospital episodes (2019–2024), mental-health programme entries, December follow-up stocks and harmonised school-support registrations to 2025. The main outcome was eligible episodes per 100 000 hospital episodes of the same panel and year. Robustness used continuously reporting panels, diagnostic position and coding-depth strata, and burden and repeat contact were also described.

Findings. Eligible hospital episodes rose from 2334 to 8731 and the indicator from 202·7 to 804·1 (95% confidence interval 787·3–821·1) per 100 000 episodes; other F80–F89 categories rose less or not at all. In 2024, 8341 of 8731 (95·5%) carried the code only secondarily, and growth persisted within every coding-depth stratum. In 2021–24, 19·1% of identifiers accounted for 40·7% of eligible episodes. Programme entries rose from 2085 (2021) to 13 155 (2025), December follow-up stocks from 3853 to 29 974, and school registrations from 21 012 to 106 786.

Interpretation. Autism is documented throughout general hospital care, not in one specialty service, and a small minority of people generated much of the recorded workload. Health systems should prepare general hospital and primary care, count people as well as episodes, and publish the unit, denominator and coverage of each indicator. These series do not measure prevalence.

Research in context
Evidence before this study

We searched PubMed and Crossref on Sept 10, 2026, without date or language limits, combining terms for autism (autism, autism spectrum disorder), routine data (administrative records, registry, diagnosis trends) and setting (Chile, Latin America), and screened the reference lists of the studies retrieved and the official documentation of each data source. National register studies from the UK, Denmark and Sweden consistently report rising recorded autism diagnoses and show that reporting rules and diagnostic practice shape those trends; they are methodologically strong, but describe high-income settings with individually linkable registers. Latin American evidence is sparser and mostly cross-sectional. We identified no study that followed several independent national administrative systems over consecutive years, or that examined whether recorded growth persists when institutional participation, diagnostic position and coding depth are held fixed.
Added value of this study

To our knowledge, this is the first study to follow autism recording simultaneously through hospital episodes, mental-health programme entries, follow-up registers and school support in a Latin American country, and to submit each series to the same robustness tests. The rise in hospital recording is not an artefact of more hospitals reporting or of longer diagnosis lists: it persists in the 65 hospitals present in every year and within every coding-depth stratum. Autism was recorded only in secondary positions in 95·5% of eligible episodes in 2024, across psychiatric, neurological, respiratory and surgical admissions. Reporting the number of contributing institutions beside every count also makes contractions visible.
Implications of all the available evidence

Autistic people are already reaching Chilean hospitals, primary care and schools in numbers several times larger than six years earlier, and general services are where they are seen. Health systems that plan autism care from routine records can prepare general hospital and primary-care teams rather than specialist services alone, and publish the unit, denominator, case definition and number of reporting institutions with every indicator, so that growth in recognition can be told apart from growth in need. Neither these series nor the available surveys establish population prevalence.
Introduction

Autistic people have diverse health, educational and support needs across the life course. Published syntheses place global prevalence near 1 in 100, with a median of 100 per 10 000 and a median male-to-female ratio of 4·2;<sup>1</sup> a three-level meta-analysis applying stricter ascertainment criteria pooled a lower figure, close to 0·7%,<sup>2</sup> and the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 estimated 61·8 million autistic people worldwide, 1 in 127, with an age-standardised prevalence of 788 per 100 000.<sup>3</sup> Much of the measured rise of recent decades is attributed to broader diagnostic criteria, greater awareness and the capacity of health and education systems to identify the condition, rather than to a change in occurrence. Chile has no comparable national estimate, so planning depends on what its institutions record. The Lancet Commission on the future of care and clinical research in autism emphasises coordination across health, education and social support, alongside heterogeneity in individual needs;<sup>4</sup> in Latin America, caregiver studies describe diagnostic delay and barriers to service access.<sup>5,6</sup>

Routine records can reveal how institutions encounter and document autism, but interpreting their growth requires attention to what is counted. A diagnosis recorded during an episode, an entry to a programme, a person registered under follow-up at a particular date, and a student receiving educational support represent different events or states. They are affected by diagnostic definitions, opportunities for service contact, and administrative coverage. Changes in these records can matter for planning even when they do not identify a change in population prevalence. International registry studies have documented substantial changes in recorded autism diagnoses and have shown that measurement and reporting practices can influence those trends.<sup>7–9</sup>

Chile provides an opportunity to study this problem across several public administrative systems. Hospital diagnosis-related-group files (GRD), Monthly Statistical Summaries (REM), and the School Integration Programme (PIE) document different aspects of institutional recording. National surveys ask about reported autism in distinct age groups. Chilean studies include an urban childhood prevalence study and a national school-registry analysis linked to regional health records, while regional caregiver research describes diagnostic delay and access barriers.<sup>5,10,11</sup> The existence of these sources does not make them interchangeable. Their different coverage, units, historical categories, and geographical assignments are part of the scientific question.

The period from 2019 to 2025 included disruption and recovery of service activity, changes in diagnostic reporting, and the introduction of Law 21.545 in 2023.<sup>12</sup> An increase in counts during this period cannot itself identify the effect of any one of these changes. We asked how administrative recording of autism changed in Chile, how robust hospital and outpatient trends were to institutional coverage, coding depth, and definition, and what complementary patterns appeared across services and territories. We centred the analysis on GRD episodes relative to hospital activity, used mental-health entries from module A05 and child/adolescent special-health-needs follow-up from module P2 as complementary indicators, and evaluated education and survey data within their own definitions. We treated territorial analyses as secondary and exploratory.
Methods
Design and sources

We conducted a national descriptive study of unlinked administrative series in Chile. GRD public-hospital episodes covered 2019–2024; REM modules contributed definition-specific periods through 2025. PIE supplied educational triangulation, and the National Disability and Dependency Survey (ENDIDE) 2022 and the National Quality of Life and Health Survey (ENCAVI) 2023–2024 supplied external population context. Supplementary figure S1 shows parallel data processing; table S1 details sources and eligibility. A written analysis plan is available from the authors; the study was not prospectively registered. Reporting followed Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) and REporting of studies Conducted using Observational Routinely-collected health Data (RECORD).<sup>13,14</sup>

The unit in GRD was an episode, including hospitalisation and major ambulatory surgery, with up to 35 diagnostic positions. The primary indicator was eligible episodes per 100 000 episodes in the same year, hospital panel, and activity category.<sup>15</sup> We separately described principal diagnosis, exclusively secondary diagnosis, strict hospitalisation, and major ambulatory surgery. Within-year identifier counts were supplementary descriptions; identifiers were not used to follow individuals across years, particularly across the format change between 2020 and 2021. Department of Health Statistics and Information (DEIS) discharges were used only as a principal-diagnosis comparison with their own discharge denominator and differing coverage.<sup>16</sup>

For clinical context, principal non-F84 categories were described among secondary-only eligible episodes, and non-F84 chapters across eligible episodes. Repeated codes within an episode were deduplicated; chapter groups could overlap. We retained the ten most frequent 2024 categories in both endpoint years (table S9). Hospital plots suppress institutions with fewer than five eligible episodes; their rates and ranks are withheld. Length of stay used episodes with valid admission and discharge dates and is reported unadjusted beside all hospitalisation episodes of the same panel and year; case mix used the relative weight of the assigned diagnosis-related group. Readmission counted any further admission within 30 days of an eligible discharge, and repeat contact counted episodes per valid identifier within the 2021–2024 era alone, because identifiers are not linked across the 2020–2021 format change.
Definitions and reporting panels

F84, pervasive developmental disorders, is a category of the disorders of psychological development block (F80–F89) within chapter V of the International Classification of Diseases, tenth revision (ICD-10), mental and behavioural disorders. Eligible hospital codes were F84 at category level and the subcodes for childhood autism (F84.0), atypical autism (F84.1), other childhood disintegrative disorder (F84.3), overactive disorder associated with intellectual disability and stereotyped movements (F84.4), Asperger syndrome (F84.5), other pervasive developmental disorders (F84.8) and pervasive developmental disorder, unspecified (F84.9). Rett syndrome (F84.2) was never an eligible code. An episode remained eligible if another selected code coexisted with F84.2; principal eligibility was determined from the principal field alone. The full F84 family and F84.0 alone were sensitivity definitions. The stable hospital panel comprised the 65 hospitals present throughout the six years. Coding depth was the number of non-empty diagnosis positions and was examined within strata as well as in selected models. None of these restrictions was interpreted as clinical validation or causal adjustment. For comparison we tabulated the remaining three-character categories of the same block (F80, F81, F82, F83, F88 and F89) across all episodes of the same panels and years, in any diagnostic position, with the same code normalisation and the same episode denominator; an episode carrying two categories contributes to both, so the categories are not mutually exclusive.

REM A05 strict-autism entries used code 05990022 from 2021; the broader diagnostic family was kept separate, including in territorial analyses. P2 used code P2500500 at the December cut in 2019–2025, with a verified expansion from ages 0–9 to 0–19 in 2021; the two age-definition eras were kept separate. P6 (REM mental-health follow-up module) strict-autism stocks used P6241010 for primary care and P6241060 for specialty care from 2021. A05 and A28 (REM rehabilitation module) were flows; P2 and P6 were cut-specific stocks, never summed across cuts. A03 (REM assessment-scale module) screening and A27 (REM health-education module) assisted referrals were described by code and definition era.<sup>17</sup> Stable REM panels required presence of the selected code in every eligible year, using the selected cut for series P. Numeric zero, a present row with an empty value, an absent row, and an establishment not observed reporting that code were recorded as distinct states. Annual presence was not interpreted as monthly completeness.
Population and educational context

Resident-denominator indicators used National Statistics Institute (INE) population projections based on the 2017 census; they were supplementary to hospital activity indicators.<sup>18</sup> Dividing records from the public network by residents does not define a population covered by those services. ENDIDE and ENCAVI estimates used their published weights, strata, and primary sampling units, with domain estimation and design-based uncertainty.<sup>19,20</sup> We distinguished eligible samples, valid responses, and positive responses. PIE autism and autism spectrum disorder (ASD)–Asperger categories were harmonised for 2019–2023 and combined with the later report of the National Higher Education Quality Assurance System (SINACES), documenting the source change and the 2022 discrepancy.<sup>21,22</sup> National Board of School Assistance and Scholarships (JUNAEB) results were not used for any estimate because outcome coding, denominator interpretation, and incomplete survey-design information limit comparability.

For survey estimation, subgroup membership entered the numerator and denominator of a weighted ratio while the full survey design was retained for variance estimation. Logit-transformed intervals used the design degrees of freedom. Missing diagnostic responses were excluded from the relevant response denominator and examined in explicit sensitivities, rather than silently recoded as negative. The physician-confirmation estimate among all ENDIDE children and the conditional proportion among children whose caregiver reported autism answer different questions and were kept separate. In administrative age–sex summaries, source marginal totals were retained; small discrepancies between age cells, sex totals, and the published aggregate were documented rather than forced to agree. Recorded sex was analysed as supplied by each source. Survey domains with fewer than 30 positive responses or relative standard error above 30% were flagged for limited precision.
Statistical and territorial analysis

We reported observed counts and indicators before model summaries. Hospital and resident-denominator indicators used exact Poisson 95% intervals; age-standardised indicators used World Health Organization (WHO) standard weights and gamma intervals.<sup>23,24</sup> These intervals describe the specified counting model, not uncertainty from incomplete administrative coverage. Selected log-linear quasi-Poisson models used a log denominator offset and Pearson dispersion; annual percent change was 100(exp(β)−1), with Wald intervals.<sup>25</sup> Hospital-year models used hospital fixed effects, with hospital-clustered standard errors in a selected sensitivity. Annual models with few observations, particularly those with additional covariates, were treated as descriptive and their non-positive results retained. Ratios of male to female counts used binomial-based intervals; indices divided each observed series by its own 2021 value, without extrapolation.

The secondary spatial analysis used GRD commune of residence, indirect age–sex standardisation, empirical-Bayes smoothing and population-weighted concentration measures, with explicit spatial weights, permutation procedures and false-discovery-rate control; Spearman coefficients were descriptive and were not presented as accounting for spatial dependence. Its full specification, sensitivities and results are in appendix methods A11 and the accompanying figures and tables.
Results
Hospital recording: magnitude, robustness and who is recorded

The observed GRD panel contained 65 hospitals in each year from 2019 to 2022, 68 in 2023 and 72 in 2024; all 65 original hospitals remained in the final year. Episodes with an eligible code in any diagnostic position increased from 2 334 among 1 151 475 episodes in 2019 to 8 731 among 1 085 813 in 2024, and the indicator from 202·7 (95% confidence interval [CI] 194·6–211·1) to 804·1 (787·3–821·1) per 100 000 GRD episodes, a 3·97-fold difference (table 1; figure 1a). The stable 65-hospital panel tracked the observed panel closely (808·6 per 100 000 episodes in 2024). Divided by the resident population and standardised to the WHO world age structure, eligible episodes rose from 15·8 (95% CI 15·2–16·5) to 59·3 (58·1–60·6) per 100 000 residents, and strict-autism programme entries from 14·3 (13·7–14·9) per 100 000 residents in 2021 to 90·2 (88·7–91·8) in 2025 (figure 1b). These are record indicators, not prevalence estimates.

Quasi-Poisson models summarised the observed indicator with an annual percent change of 35·9% (95% CI 30·0–42·1), with similar estimates for the stable panel, for 2021–2024 alone and for strict hospitalisation (figure 1c; table S2). Mean coding depth increased from 4·39 to 5·78 diagnoses per episode, yet the indicator rose within every coding-depth stratum, between 3·6-fold and 5·0-fold among episodes with three to ten diagnoses, and the depth-adjusted model gave 46·9% (40·8–53·3) (figure S2a). Robustness was not uniform: the principal-diagnosis indicator rose more modestly, from 19·8 (95% CI 17·3–22·5) to 35·9 (32·4–39·7) per 100 000 episodes, and the specification that included both coding depth and the 2020–2021 indicator gave −2·4% (−20·1 to 19·2) with two residual degrees of freedom; this imprecise, non-positive estimate is retained (figure S8b). The increase was also specific to autism within its diagnostic block: on the same denominator, mixed specific developmental disorders (F83) rose 3·35-fold, disorders of scholastic skills (F81) 1·80-fold and speech and language disorders (F80) 1·78-fold, while F82 and F89 were unchanged, against 3·97-fold for autism (figure 1d). The independent DEIS discharge series moved in the same direction (figure S2d), and hospital heterogeneity remained substantial: among 72 hospitals in 2024 the median indicator was 638·0 per 100 000 episodes (interquartile range 393·3–976·1; maximum 5 210·7; figure S2c).

Growth was faster among females than males. The male-to-female ratio of eligible episodes fell from 3·27 (95% CI 2·97–3·60) in 2019 to 2·03 (1·94–2·13) in 2024, and the ratio of strict-autism programme entries from 3·52 (3·17–3·92) in 2021 to 2·07 (1·99–2·14) in 2025 (figure 1e); age-standardised episode indicators rose from 23·8 to 79·0 per 100 000 male residents and from 7·6 to 39·0 per 100 000 female residents, with annual changes of 37·5% (33·6–41·5) and 54·9% (48·3–61·8) (figure S3). Recording remained concentrated in childhood and adolescence, with a growing adolescent and adult share: in 2024, 47·7% of the 8 728 episodes with known age involved children aged 0–9 years, 40·8% those aged 10–19 years and 11·5% adults, against 55·7%, 33·2% and 11·1% in 2019. Resident-denominated episode indicators rose in every age group, by 143% at ages 0–4 years, 420% at 15–19 years and 362% at 20–24 years (figure 1f), and episodes at age 20 years or older rose from 260 to 1 004. Programme entries shifted likewise, with adult A05 entries rising from 121 to 1 205 (table S7).
Clinical profile of the hospital episodes

Autism was recorded overwhelmingly as an accompanying condition rather than as the reason for admission: 2 106 of 2 334 eligible episodes (90·2%) carried the code only in a secondary position in 2019 and 8 341 of 8 731 (95·5%) in 2024 (figure 2a). Among these secondary-only episodes in 2024, the most frequent principal three-character categories were depressive episode (380, 4·6%), redundant prepuce, phimosis or paraphimosis (373, 4·5%), epilepsy (358, 4·3%) and acute appendicitis (324, 3·9%); no category reached 5%. Their composition changed: depressive episodes rose from 22 of 2 106 (1·0%) to 380 of 8 341 (4·6%), whereas epilepsy rose in count, from 152 to 358, but fell in share from 7·2% to 4·3% (figure 2b; table S9). Non-F84 mental and behavioural chapters rose from 25·4% to 40·6% of eligible episodes and respiratory chapters from 26·2% to 34·6%, while nervous-system chapters fell from 26·1% to 17·9% despite increasing from 609 to 1 566 episodes (figure S9a).

Eligible episodes also became less distinctive from the rest of hospital activity. Among hospitalisation episodes, mean length of stay fell from 9·4 days in 2019 to 7·7 in 2024 while the mean for all hospitalisation episodes in the same panel rose from 6·7 to 7·1, and the mean relative weight of the diagnosis-related group fell from 0·84 to 0·81 (figure 2c). Episodes with autism as principal diagnosis stayed longer, 16·1 days in 2019 and 13·4 in 2024, than secondary-only episodes, 8·6 and 7·3 days (figure S9b), unstandardised for age, case mix or hospital. Recorded contact was repeated and concentrated: within 30 days of an eligible discharge, 15·1% (95% CI 13·7–16·6) were followed by an all-cause readmission in 2019 and 12·7% (12·0–13·4) in 2024, and 21·9% (20·3–23·6) and 19·6% (18·6–20·6) within 90 days; most readmissions again carried an eligible code (10·3% of discharges at 30 days in 2024). In the validated identifier era 2021–2024, 15 670 identifiers accounted for 21 374 eligible episodes: 19·1% of identifiers accounted for 40·7% of episodes, and the 189 identifiers with six or more episodes (1·2%) for 1 852 episodes (8·7%) (figure 2d). Identifiers are not linked across the 2020–2021 format change, so these describe contact within one era.

The growth was concentrated in the specific childhood-autism code. Among coded eligible subcodes, F84.0 rose from 59·0% in 2019 to 82·3% in 2024, unspecified pervasive developmental disorder (F84.9) stayed between 8% and 11%, and Asperger syndrome (F84.5) fell from 17·2% to 1·6%, from 409 to 139 records; an episode can carry more than one eligible subcode (figure 2e). Across the full period, 297 Rett-only episodes were excluded and 30 with Rett and another eligible code retained; the F84.0-only definition reached 665·9 per 100 000 episodes in 2024 (figure S8a; table S2).
The community care pathway and the period of Law 21.545

Primary-care screening records expanded with the 2023 introduction of Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised with Follow-Up (M-CHAT-R/F) codes. First-stage results rose from 19 632 in 2023 to 25 074 in 2024 (low risk 14 083 to 18 142; medium risk 3 642 to 4 698; high risk 1 907 to 2 234), high-risk results with specialist referral from 1 152 to 1 741, second-stage referrals from 1 136 to 2 283, and suspected autism identified in other consultations from 8 221 to 12 281 (figure 3a). These aggregated items are annual flows from different establishments; they cannot be linked into an individual cascade or converted into positivity or referral completion (figure S4c; table S4B).

Strict-autism A05 programme entries increased from 2 085 in 2021 to 4 640 in 2022, 8 049 in 2023, 11 842 in 2024 and 13 155 in 2025, while clinical discharges rose from 494 to 3 367 (figure 3b; table 2). Within 258 establishments with an eligible row every year, entries increased from 1 522 to 6 767, a 4·45-fold change against 6·31-fold in the observed network (figure S4a). People under control in December rose from 2 257 to 21 843 in primary care and from 3 562 to 12 645 in specialty care (figure 3c), with annual changes of 41·7% (95% CI 35·4–48·3) and 21·9% (18·4–25·5). P2 follow-up of autism among children with special health-care needs, whose age universe widened from younger than 10 years to younger than 20 years in 2021, rose from 3 853 to 29 974 within the latter era and from 1 748 to 9 128 in the same 193 establishments (figure S4b). Rehabilitation entries, first recorded in 2023, rose from 3 962 to 15 859 at the primary level and from 731 to 1 740 at the hospital level, whereas counselling and assisted referral in the screening context peaked in 2024 (3 874 and 1 068) and fell in 2025 (3 026 and 878) (figure 3d).

Law 21.545, published in March 2023, is a documented change in the institutional environment rather than an intervention that this design can evaluate. The new screening codes, the 2024–2025 redesign of the M-CHAT-R/F items and the rehabilitation entry codes entered the REM during its implementation (figure S4c), and every programme indicator continued to rise through 2025. The relative growth nevertheless decelerated as the period advanced: entries rose by 123%, 73%, 47% and 11% in successive years from 2022 to 2025, and the P2 December stock by 106%, 66%, 65% and 38%. Without a counterfactual these series neither support nor exclude an effect of the law; they show that recording expanded before its publication and that the pace of expansion slowed while it was being implemented.
Convergence across systems and population context

Educational recording rose faster than the School Integration Programme as a whole. Harmonised autism registrations increased from 21 012 in 2019 to 63 642 in 2023 while total PIE enrolment grew from 385 995 to 473 006, so the autism share rose from 5·44% to 13·45%; the harmonised series reached 106 786 in 2025 (figure 4a; table S5). With 2021 as 100, GRD episode indicators reached 278 in 2024, DEIS principal-diagnosis discharges 200, A05 entries 568 (631 in 2025), the P2 December stock 564 (778), primary-care follow-up 706 (968) and PIE registrations 280 (346); equal indices do not imply equal levels or coverage (figure 4b).

Two national surveys provide population context that administrative series cannot supply. ENDIDE 2022 estimated reported autism at 2·87% (95% CI 2·37–3·47) among children aged 2–17 years, 4·57% among boys and 1·11% among girls, and 0·29% (0·22–0·38) among adults; the child estimate requiring reported physician confirmation was 2·39% (1·94–2·95). ENCAVI 2023–2024 estimated a diagnosis in 0·71% (0·50–1·01) of people aged 15 years or older (figure 4c; table S3). The surveys differ from each other, and from the administrative series, in question wording, age universe, respondent and denominator; they are not used to validate records, and no share of autistic people reaching services is estimated from them.

Hospital recording became geographically less concentrated: communes with eligible records increased from 242 to 302 of 346 between 2019 and 2024, and the population-weighted Gini coefficient declined from 0·373 to 0·299 (figure S6). Across communes in the common 2021–2024 window, hospital episode and programme entry indicators were only weakly aligned (Spearman ρ = 0·34 in 157 communes, and 0·24 when the Metropolitan Region was excluded), and the P2 stock aligned weakly with both (ρ = 0·11 and 0·32) (figure 4d; figure S7; table S6). These descriptive coefficients carry no spatial inference.
Discussion

Autism recording expanded substantially and simultaneously across Chile's hospital, outpatient, follow-up and school-support records between 2019 and 2025. Hospital episodes carrying an eligible code rose almost fourfold relative to hospital activity, and the 2024 indicator in the 65 hospitals that reported in every year matched the indicator in the observed network, so the increase is not explained by hospitals joining the system. Mental-health programme entries rose 4·45-fold and December follow-up stocks more than fivefold within establishments that reported continuously and within a single age-definition era, and school registrations rose about fivefold. What these series measure is administrative recognition and recorded demand; they do not quantify how much of the change comes from reporting, diagnosis, coding, service use, or the underlying population. Recorded episodes also became shorter and less complex, and a small minority of people accounted for a large share of them. The increase was also concentrated in the most specific diagnostic code rather than in unspecified ones.

The predominance of secondary hospital coding places the increase within general health care. Principal diagnoses included psychiatric, neurological, respiratory and surgical categories, with no single category dominating. This diversity matters for planning because autistic patients can require care throughout the hospital, beyond services organised around autism as a principal diagnosis. Recorded co-diagnoses are nevertheless shaped by clinical contact and documentation. Their frequencies cannot establish excess comorbidity risk, severity or unmet need without a comparison population and clinical assessment. Repeated episodes contribute to workload but do not represent new diagnoses.

The clinical profile of a recorded episode changed as recording expanded. Eligible hospitalisations lasted almost three days longer than the average hospitalisation in 2019 and barely longer than it in 2024, and the mean relative weight of their diagnosis-related group fell over the same period. The simplest reading is that the episodes being captured moved from the most complex towards the ordinary, which is what broader recognition would produce. It is not the only reading: case mix, age structure, admission thresholds during the pandemic and coding practice all changed at once, and we did not standardise for them. The concentration of repeat contact is less exposed to those explanations, because it is internal to the recorded population. One in five identifiers accounted for two in five episodes, and 189 people accounted for 8·7% of all eligible episodes over four years. Service planning that counts episodes will therefore overstate the number of people to be served, and planning that counts people will understate the workload; both figures are needed, and only the second is usually published. The distinction between the national hospital indicator and the distribution of hospital indicators also matters for interpretation. The national value weights hospitals by their total activity; the median summarises the hospital distribution with equal weight for each institution. Their difference does not identify inadequate care or excess autism risk. Hospitals differ in referral roles, the ages and conditions treated, and documentation practices. The displayed variation therefore motivates examination of local service context before allocating resources according to a national average. Stable-panel agreement establishes neither comparable capture across hospitals nor uniform capacity within them (figure S2ca).

Three features of the data make reporting artefact an insufficient explanation, without making it irrelevant. First, growth persisted within coding-depth strata. Iezzoni and colleagues showed that additional diagnosis fields alone do not ensure complete comorbidity capture; Song and colleagues found that recorded diagnoses varied with local practice intensity.<sup>26,27</sup> Depth also reflects clinical complexity and hospital organisation, so stratification changes the episodes compared. Second, growth persisted within establishments that reported in every year, although stable panels answer a narrower question than complete service coverage: an establishment can contribute an annual row while lacking records in other months, and can change its catchment, staffing, coding and reporting intensity, while a missing row need not mean that no care occurred. Follow-up stocks additionally depend on entry, exit, transfer and retention, and must be read as the number recorded at each cut, with no observed individual transition between modules. Third, restriction to a single age-definition era and to known cells for children younger than 10 years retained an increasing follow-up trajectory within recurring establishments, although neither sensitivity resolves empty age cells or changes in follow-up practice. None of these comparisons is a causal decomposition. With six annual observations, adjustment for mean coding depth and the 2020–2021 disruption cannot recover a counterfactual without changes in coding, and the imprecise, non-positive principal-diagnosis sensitivity limits a uniform-growth narrative. The administrative picture also contains contractions, with fewer mental-health reporting establishments and fewer assisted referrals in 2025, so entries, stocks and reporting coverage are more informative monitored together than as a single aggregate growth estimate.

The time pattern does not show a discontinuity aligned with the 2023 law. Year-on-year growth in strict-autism programme entries was 123% in 2022, 73% in 2023, 47% in 2024 and 11% in 2025, and December follow-up stocks grew by 106%, 66%, 65% and 38% across the same years; educational registrations grew fastest between 2022 and 2023 and more slowly in each later year. Growth decelerated as the policy period advanced. This description neither supports nor excludes an effect of Law 21.545: the series are short, pandemic recovery overlaps the policy period, REM definitions changed within it, and no comparison group is available. We report the pattern because a reader will look for it, not because this design can attribute it.

The changing sex composition warrants attention because administrative recognition is age dependent. Loomes and colleagues found lower male predominance in studies that actively screened populations than in those restricted to existing diagnoses.<sup>28</sup> More recently, Swedish longitudinal records showed later diagnostic peaks among females and sex ratios that varied with age and period.<sup>29</sup> These findings support examining age alongside sex in Chilean surveillance; they do not establish that our declining record ratio measures a change in the population sex ratio. Age-specific profiles and clinical context add different information to surveillance: the former locate recorded demand along the life course, whereas the latter describe the contacts in which an eligible code is documented. Their joint presentation supports planning across paediatric, adolescent and adult services without implying that the same individuals moved between those services. Neither the age shift nor changing diagnostic proportions can distinguish changes in recognition from changes in underlying morbidity.

The contribution relative to earlier Chilean evidence is therefore specific. Roman-Urrestarazu and colleagues linked the 2021 national school registry with clinical records from Araucanía Sur and used Bayesian modelling to estimate national autism prevalence and unmet special-education needs.<sup>11</sup> Their study already brought education and health together. Our study addresses change over successive years, with hospital activity as the primary denominator and explicit hospital and establishment panels, diagnostic-position restrictions, coding-depth comparisons, and REM definition eras. We do not reproduce their linked design or infer prevalence from concordant trends. The two approaches answer different questions: the estimated population burden and educational support gap, versus the evolution and interpretability of routine recording. International studies show why these distinctions matter. United Kingdom primary-care data documented increasing recorded diagnoses, with different changes by age and sex; Danish analyses examined identifiable changes in diagnostic and reporting rules; and Swedish data distinguished changes in registered diagnosis from changes in the measured autism phenotype.<sup>7–9</sup> These results make changes in recognition and recording plausible explanations, but their effect sizes cannot be transferred to Chile. Education and surveys situate these service records within broader institutional and population contexts. The growing autism share within PIE cannot be described solely by expansion of overall programme enrolment, although historical categories and the source transition remain relevant. These sources provide neither clinical validation of hospital codes nor a multiplier for unrecorded service need.

Several limitations remain unresolved by sensitivity analysis. Neither GRD nor REM supplies a nationally validated population at risk for autism ascertainment. Public-network records omit activity outside the included systems and can include repeated contacts. No clinical validation of the eligible codes was undertaken. Pandemic-related changes coincide with evolving coverage, coding, and policy, and the final REM year has fewer A05 reporting establishments despite national presence in every month. Stable panels are selected institutional subsets rather than representative samples. The short time series make adjusted slopes sensitive to specification; conventional intervals address model uncertainty and not the full uncertainty of coverage, measurement, or dependence. The study was not prospectively registered. The territorial analyses reported in the appendix carry further limitations: GRD is assigned by recorded residence and REM to the establishment, and referral patterns, the concentration of specialist services and shared denominators can all affect ecological associations.

A six-country caregiver study reported mean ages of 22·4 months at first concerns and 46·3 months at diagnosis, placing expanding records within a potentially prolonged process of recognition and access.<sup>5</sup> The Lancet Commission emphasises diverse needs across the life course and coordination between health, education and social services.<sup>4</sup> For planning, these priorities favour tracking recorded workload together with age, support needs and service continuity, rather than treating an administrative total as a sufficient measure of care. Surveillance should therefore publish definitions, denominators and reporting coverage alongside workload, using age and service setting to guide capacity assessment. Law 21.545 provides policy context, but this design does not estimate its effect.<sup>12</sup> For health systems in the Americas that plan autism care from routine records, the practical implication is immediate: prepare general hospital and primary-care teams rather than specialist services alone, and publish the unit, denominator, case definition and number of reporting institutions with every count. Clinical code validation, repeated population measurement and ethically governed linkage would then help distinguish recognition, repeated use, continuity of care and unmet need.

Scope and reading guide

This supplement provides the scientific definitions, estimators and selected complementary results for the bilingual article. Tables and figure labels have the same numbering in both languages. GRD denotes hospital diagnosis-related groups; REM denotes Monthly Statistical Summaries; PIE denotes the School Integration Programme; NANEAS denotes children and adolescents with special health-care needs. All displayed intervals are 95% unless stated otherwise.
A. Extended methods
A1. Study design, sources and observation units

This is a repeated cross-sectional study of administrative recording across Chilean health and education systems, with external population-survey context. The hospital core comprises public-hospital diagnosis-related group (GRD) episodes in 2019–2024. Complementary health-service series come from Monthly Statistical Summaries (REM), with available periods determined by the module and diagnostic era. The School Integration Programme (PIE) provides educational administrative triangulation in 2019–2025. The National Disability and Dependency Survey (ENDIDE) 2022 and the National Quality of Life and Health Survey (ENCAVI) 2023–2024 describe different survey populations and questions. The study estimates recorded activity, follow-up stocks and administrative indicators; it does not estimate the population prevalence or incidence of clinically validated autism.<sup>1,2</sup>

GRD observations are episodes, REM observations are establishment–month–code records or establishment-specific semester cuts, and educational observations are the published school-registration totals. These sources were not linked at the individual level. Similar trends therefore cannot establish that the same people progressed through screening, referral, entry and follow-up. The availability of a record in one system does not imply inclusion in another. Hospital episode identifiers support within-year person counts only under the restrictions below. Survey design, educational harmonisation and territorial methods are described separately because their observation units, denominators and coverage differ.

Figure S1 summarises independent processing streams rather than a participant cohort. The six GRD files contained 5 808 535 activity episodes. Applying the eligible-code rule retained 25 323 episodes: 1 617 with an eligible principal diagnosis and 23 706 with eligible diagnoses exclusively in secondary positions. Of 327 episodes mentioning Rett, 297 had no other eligible code and were excluded; 30 remained eligible. The 297 Rett-only episodes remained in the overall hospital activity denominator. Hospital comparisons use the numerator and denominator for the same year, hospital panel and activity modality; valid identifiers support person counts only within each year. A05 (REM mental-health entry module) aggregates known monthly totals of code 05990022 as an annual flow, while P2 (REM child/adolescent special-health-needs follow-up module) selects P2500500 at December as a stock. Stable A05 membership requires at least one selected-code row in every year of 2021–2025; stable P2 membership requires a December row in every year of 2019–2025. Missing cells, absent rows and true zero values retain distinct meanings. The P2 age-universe change in 2021 is treated as a definition break, with same-era and under-10 analyses. PIE categories are harmonised within documented source eras. ENDIDE and ENCAVI use their eligible age and valid-response domains, weights, strata and primary sampling units; they provide external population context and are not clinical validation of administrative records.
A2. Hospital eligibility, position, activity and identifiers

F84, pervasive developmental disorders, is a category of the disorders of psychological development block (F80–F89) of chapter V of the tenth revision of the International Classification of Diseases, mental and behavioural disorders. The selected hospital definition comprises the exact codes F84 at category level, F84.0 childhood autism, F84.1 atypical autism, F84.3 other childhood disintegrative disorder, F84.4 overactive disorder associated with intellectual disability and stereotyped movements, F84.5 Asperger syndrome, F84.8 other pervasive developmental disorders and F84.9 pervasive developmental disorder, unspecified, in any of 35 diagnostic positions. F84.2 is Rett syndrome. Codes were standardised to uppercase with punctuation and spaces removed before exact matching. F84.2, Rett syndrome, does not confer eligibility. However, an episode with another eligible diagnosis remains included when F84.2 coexists. This is removal of Rett as an eligible code, not exclusion of everyone whose episode mentions Rett. F84.0 alone and the broader F84 family including F84.2 are separate definition sensitivities; neither replaces the selected numerator.

Principal diagnosis means an eligible code in the first diagnostic position, whether or not another eligible code appears secondarily. Exclusively secondary diagnosis means eligibility in positions 2–35 with no eligible code in the first position. The principal and exclusively secondary categories are mutually exclusive and sum to the any-position count. Episodes with principal Rett and an eligible secondary diagnosis contribute to the any-position and secondary-only categories, but not to the selected principal category. In 2024, 94 episodes mentioned Rett: 87 had no other eligible code and were excluded; seven remained eligible through a coexisting code.

The primary denominator is all GRD episodes in the corresponding hospital panel and year. Hospitalisation and major ambulatory surgery are analysed separately with their own modality denominators. A residual activity category occurs in 2019 but has no records in 2020–2024; its absence is not a zero-valued rate. Coding depth is the number of nonempty diagnostic fields per episode. The coding-stratum comparison divides eligible episodes by all episodes in the same stratum; the inset presents descriptive mean depth. Within-year person counts use valid identifiers, excluding missing or explicitly uninformative identifiers. Identifier encoding changes between 2020 and 2021, with no shared eligible identifiers across that boundary, and the variable name changes in 2024. Counts were not summed across years as unique people and do not define a longitudinal cohort.

For the existing hospital clinical-context analysis, diagnoses other than F84 were reduced to three-character International Classification of Diseases, tenth revision (ICD-10) categories. Within each eligible episode, duplicate occurrences of the same category were removed separately for principal, secondary and any-position tabulations. Principal diagnoses among secondary-only eligible episodes describe the recorded main diagnosis at that contact. Chapter summaries count an episode once per chapter, even if several codes from that chapter occur. Chapters can overlap within an episode. We selected the ten most frequent principal categories and chapters in 2024 and retained the same categories in the 2019 comparison; no significance test or new risk model selected them. Denominators were independently checked against the hospital core in every year. Clinical descriptions refer to administrative coding and are not a validation of diagnoses or an estimate of comorbidity in autistic residents.
A3. REM definitions, diagnostic eras, flows and stocks

A05 strict-autism entries use code 05990022 from 2021 and are annual sums of the reported both-sex total. The broader post-2021 pervasive-developmental-disorder family includes autism, Asperger syndrome, childhood disintegrative disorder and unspecified pervasive developmental disorder; the Rett entry category, 05990024, is excluded from the selected family sensitivity. These broader totals are not labelled strict autism. Broad A05 code 06902600 in 2019–2020 cannot be separated into the later strict categories and is not joined to the strict-autism series. A05 discharges are separate flows and do not imply that an identified entrant subsequently left care.

P2 code P2500500 records autism within the population of children and adolescents with special health-care needs under follow-up. Full age-column inspection identified an expansion in its reporting universe: the 2019–2020 layout covers children younger than 10 years, whereas the 2021–2025 layout includes ages 10–14 and 15–19 years, extending the universe to younger than 20 years. The reported total and the unchanged code therefore do not form an age-comparable 2019–2025 series. Figures separate the two eras; the main post-expansion comparison is 2021–2025. December is the principal cut and June is shown separately. Counts at different cuts are never summed as unique people.

A bounded common-age P2 sensitivity sums known age–sex cells for children younger than 10 years, using the same age-by-sex cells in every December file. The sums equal the reported total in 2019–2020. After expansion they exclude the newly represented adolescent groups; rows with all those age cells empty remain missing rather than being assigned zero. The sensitivity reports both the known-age sums and their missingness. P6 (REM mental-health follow-up module) primary-care and specialty stocks similarly remain distinct: broad codes P6223000 and P6223380 in 2019–2020 are separated from strict-autism codes P6241010 and P6241060 in 2021–2025. A28 (REM rehabilitation module) primary-care and hospital rehabilitation entries, codes 29101629 and 29101651, are annual flows in 2023–2025. They are not stocks or linked transitions.
A4. Stable panels, missingness and 2025 availability

The hospital stable panel contains the 65 hospital identifiers present in every year of 2019–2022; all 65 also contribute in 2023 and 2024, making this set identical to the six-year intersection. The annual observed network expands to 68 hospitals in 2023 and 72 in 2024. A05 stable membership requires at least one strict-code row in every year 2021–2025, yielding 258 establishments. The original P2 December intersection across 2019–2025 contains 193 establishments; it is retained as a fixed-establishment sensitivity but does not correct the 2021 age expansion. Restricting the membership window to the comparable 2021–2025 era yields 433 establishments, reported as an additional bounded sensitivity.

Annual row presence, a known value, a recorded zero and complete monthly reporting are different properties. Known numeric totals are summed; empty cells remain missing, and a group containing no known total is missing. Explicit zeros are retained. An absent establishment-month cannot distinguish inactivity, an omitted zero or nonreporting and is not imputed as zero. National A05 strict-code records span all 12 months each year, yet only 2, 5, 14, 29 and 55 establishments respectively have a row in every month of 2021–2025. These figures describe stored-row presence, not a reporting-compliance rate. One A05 total cell is empty in 2024 and one in 2025.

The selected A05, P6 and A28 code layouts are compatible between 2024 and 2025, and the earlier P2 age change is documented separately. National availability does not prove that all eligible establishments submitted complete data. In particular, A05 annual reporters fall from 1 070 in 2024 to 952 in 2025 despite increasing totals. Neither a stable panel nor an establishment offset identifies the fraction of growth attributable to expanding coverage, activity, diagnostic recognition or recording practices.
A5. Denominators and population compatibility

The central hospital indicator is activity-denominated: its denominator is observed GRD episodes, not residents, beneficiaries or hospitals. Population-denominated age and sex indicators instead use National Statistics Institute (INE) resident-population projections, base 2017, at 30 June, matched by year and age–sex group. Their numerators are public-network records. The population actually covered by the reporting network is not established, so these indicators are not autism prevalence or risk within a known covered population. A05 is located by establishment, whereas GRD territorial analysis uses recorded residence. Dividing establishment-based REM counts by residents does not ensure that numerator and denominator refer to the same people.<sup>3</sup>

Beneficiary totals, primary-care enrolment, resident populations and numbers of reporting establishments represent distinct reference quantities. They are not interchangeable denominators or components of a mutually exclusive partition of the Chilean population. Denominator sensitivities retain their original timing and geographic definition and are interpreted within their own estimands. Ratios per establishment describe recorded volume per reporting site, not individual risk; a hospital activity denominator describes the share of episodes with an eligible code, not the fraction of all residents who have autism.
A6. Rates, standardisation, uncertainty, sex ratios and indices

Unstandardised indicators are 100 000 times the observed count divided by the corresponding positive denominator. Exact Poisson 95% limits for the count are divided by that same denominator. The age displays aggregate five-year groups through ages 40–44 and combine older ages as 45 years or older, retaining the original hospital display’s age structure. Direct standardisation uses 17 age groups: five-year groups from 0–4 through 75–79 years and an 80-years-or-older group, weighted by the normalised World Health Organization (WHO) world standard. Fay–Feuer gamma intervals are retained. All displayed sex-year standardised estimates and interval endpoints were recalculated from the preserved age cells and INE denominators and agreed numerically with the source outputs.<sup>4,5</sup>

A05’s reported both-sex, reported sex-specific and age-cell totals were not forced to agree. Male age cells sum to one more record than the reported male total in 2022, and female age cells do so in 2024. In 2025, reported male and female totals sum to 13 156 versus 13 155 in the both-sex field. Flow totals use the both-sex field; sex-count ratios use the reported sex totals; age-specific and standardised indicators use age-cell sums. The three one-record discrepancies are disclosed because an assumed reconciliation would alter the source without evidence.

The male:female recording ratio is M/F, not an adjusted rate ratio. Its displayed interval transforms exact binomial limits for M/(M+F) to odds; the independent-record model does not accommodate repeated contacts or clustering. Indexed trajectories use 2021=100, the first common year, and display the shared 2021–2024 window: GRD is the activity-denominated rate, A05 is the annual entry count, P2 is the December stock within the post-expansion age universe, and PIE is the harmonised educational stock. An index compares relative change, not levels or equivalent populations; absent years are not extrapolated.

The intervals reported for administrative indicators describe the specified counting model. They do not cover coding error, undercapture, or dependence introduced by repeated contacts of the same person. Survey intervals cover sampling variation under the declared complex design; they do not cover diagnostic validity of the reported answer.

Here k=100,000, C<sub>a</sub> is the observed count, N<sub>a</sub> the corresponding resident population, and w<sub>a</sub> the normalised standard weight in age group a. The gamma upper limit uses the maximum w<sub>a</sub>/N<sub>a</sub> correction. All displayed groups have a valid positive population denominator. These intervals condition on observed denominators and do not account for repeated episodes, reporting error or incomplete network capture.
X<sub>s,t</sub> is the selected observed quantity for source s in year t; each source retains its original unit before indexing.

supplement.html: A7. Selected trend models and interpretation of sensitivity analyses

The retained trend models use a Poisson mean with log link and Pearson-scale dispersion estimation, conventionally described as quasi-Poisson log-linear models. The annual count is the outcome; time is years since the first year of the fitted window. The log denominator enters as a fixed-coefficient offset. National GRD models use matching episode counts as offsets, separate any-position and principal outcomes, and compare observed and stable panels and all activity with strict hospitalisation. Selected covariates are mean diagnostic depth among all episodes, centred within the model window, and an indicator for 2020–2021. These are descriptive adjustments and are not causal intervention terms.<sup>6</sup>

Hospital–year models include hospital indicator variables and a common time slope, with log hospital-year episodes as the offset. The selected robust specification clusters standard errors by hospital, allowing dependence within hospitals; it does not correct unknown cross-hospital dependence. Hospital-depth-adjusted specifications in the original analysis use model-based Pearson-scale standard errors and must not be described as hospital-clustered. National models likewise do not estimate a serial-correlation structure. Pearson dispersion and chronological deviance-residual Durbin–Watson summaries remain diagnostics, not evidence that the assumptions are satisfied.

Selected A05 models compare resident-population offsets, reporting-establishment offsets and stable-panel counts in 2021–2025; these estimate different quantities. P2 trend summaries are restricted to the comparable 2021–2025 age era, with count and establishment-offset specifications. Previously generated models spanning the 2021 P2 age expansion are not retained as estimates of a comparable full-period trend. Four to seven annual observations, and sometimes only two residual degrees of freedom after adjustment, make model-based intervals and p values fragile. The principal-diagnosis GRD model with depth and the 2020–2021 indicator is retained despite its uncertain annual percent change (APC) of −2·4% (95% interval −20·1 to 19·2). Stable-panel persistence or a positive adjusted coefficient does not identify how much of the observed increase each mechanism explains.
Selection is based on the question, validity and nonredundancy, not statistical significance; conflicting and null sensitivities are retained.

Y<sub>t</sub> is the recorded annual count, D<sub>t</sub> its specified denominator and Z<sub>t</sub> the selected covariate vector. With no offset, D<sub>t</sub>=1. Annual percent change (APC) intervals transform beta plus or minus 1·96 standard errors. They summarise a fitted log-linear trajectory, not an identified mechanism of change.

supplement.html: A8. Population surveys and design-based estimation

The population context comprises ENDIDE 2022 and ENCAVI 2023–24, analysed separately. ENDIDE targets people aged 2 years or older living in private dwellings, excluding hard-to-access areas outside its INE sampling frame. The selected-person file contains 35 536 respondents: 30 010 adults aged 18 years or older and 5 526 children aged 2–17 years. Adult autism reporting used c26_33 and child reporting used n29_19 (1=yes, 0=no); the latter was answered by the principal responsible adult. The adult module could be self-completed, assisted or answered through a third party. These labels identify a reported health condition and do not imply independent clinical assessment. No selected respondent lacked the autism item for their applicable module. Among children with autism reported, n29a_19 asks whether a doctor had said the child had autism; 1 denotes yes, 2 no and −99 nonresponse. The conditional primary denominator includes only valid yes/no answers. A separate estimate divides the number with both report and medical confirmation by the entire child domain, and a sensitivity analysis counts confirmation nonresponse as unconfirmed in the reporter domain.<sup>7–9</sup>

ENCAVI targets usual residents aged 15 years or older in occupied private dwellings in Chile’s 16 regions. The diagnosis item p4_6_1_h asks whether the respondent has been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder; the questionnaire specifies a conventional medical diagnosis. The primary domain includes responses 1=yes or 2=no. Responses 8=do not know and 9=no response were excluded from that domain, while all sampling units were retained for variance estimation. A sensitivity analysis counts these responses as no reported diagnosis. Of 16 590 respondents, 16 484 provided a valid response, with 101 “do not know” and five nonresponses. The surveys differ in ages, questions, respondent type and year; estimates are not directly standardised to a common survey population and are not validation of GRD or REM.

Each survey proportion is the weighted ratio p̂<sub>D</sub> = Σ<sub>i</sub> w<sub>i</sub> D<sub>i</sub> y<sub>i</sub> / Σ<sub>i</sub> w<sub>i</sub> D<sub>i</sub>, where w<sub>i</sub> is the expansion weight, D<sub>i</sub> indicates membership in the analysis domain and y<sub>i</sub> is the binary response. ENDIDE uses fexp, estrato and cod_upm; ENCAVI uses w_personas_cal, varstrat and varunit. The variance uses Taylor linearisation with u<sub>i</sub> = w<sub>i</sub> D<sub>i</sub>(y<sub>i</sub>−p̂<sub>D</sub>)/Σ<sub>i</sub> w<sub>i</sub>D<sub>i</sub> and primary-sampling-unit totals within strata. Units outside a domain contribute zero rather than being deleted. A with-replacement first-stage variance is calculated as Σ<sub>h</sub> m<sub>h</sub>/(m<sub>h</sub>−1) Σ<sub>j</sub>(U<sub>hj</sub>−Ū<sub>h</sub>)², where m<sub>h</sub> is the number of primary sampling units (PSUs) in stratum h and U<sub>hj</sub>=Σ<sub>i</sub>∈hj u<sub>i</sub>. No finite-population correction is applied. Confidence limits use the logit transform and a t critical value with degrees of freedom equal to PSUs minus strata. The realised designs contain 8 477 PSUs in 32 strata for ENDIDE and 350 PSUs in 96 strata for ENCAVI; neither contains a singleton stratum. Weighted population totals are expansion-weight sums, and unweighted positive counts divided by domain sample size do not reproduce weighted percentages. Small subgroup cells (<30 positives) or relative standard error >30% were flagged as imprecise. The four national/domain estimates in figure 4c do not meet these flags.

We used the survey questions to define distinct reporting domains before examining age or sex. ENDIDE separates adults reporting autism, children with reported autism, and children whose report also includes physician confirmation. Confirmation is reported by the respondent and was not independently reassessed. Age and sex estimates were calculated within each domain using the complete survey design, retaining out-of-domain sampling units for variance estimation. The supplemental table reports weighted percentages alongside unweighted valid and positive counts, design-based confidence intervals and relative standard errors. Estimates with fewer than 30 positive responses or relative standard error above 30% remain visible but receive a precision warning. No regional or communal survey estimates were produced.

supplement.html: Cross-system indices and sex composition

Trajectories were indexed descriptively as I<sub>st</sub> = 100 X<sub>st</sub>/X<sub>s,2021</sub> over the common 2021–24 window. X is the GRD rate per hospital activity, the strict A05 annual entry count, the P2 December children and adolescents with special health-care needs (NANEAS) stock for ages 0–19 years, or the harmonised PIE annual stock. P2’s age universe expands from 0–9 years in the 2019–20 dictionaries to 0–19 years from 2021; therefore the common 2021–24 index is calculated wholly within the expanded era. A stable establishment panel cannot correct this change in age eligibility. Thus an equal index measures equal relative change within each source, not an equal level or common population. No missing year was extrapolated. Male-to-female composition is the count ratio R<sub>t</sub>=M<sub>t</sub>/F<sub>t</sub> among records with those sex codes; it is not a ratio of sex-standardised population rates. Model-based 95% intervals transform exact Clopper–Pearson limits for p<sub>t</sub>=M<sub>t</sub>/(M<sub>t</sub>+F<sub>t</sub>) using p<sub>t</sub>/(1−p<sub>t</sub>), conditional on the sex-coded record total and an independent-binomial model. These intervals do not account for repeated contacts, hospital/facility clustering or coding error. GRD excludes records with unknown sex from this ratio; A05 uses the explicitly reported sex totals, which differ from some age-cell sums by one record in 2022, 2024 and 2025. In 2025 the reported male plus female total exceeds the both-sex A05 total by one. These source inconsistencies were preserved and the aggregate A05 flow uses its reported both-sex total.
A9. Educational harmonisation

The PIE series follows the administrative programme rather than a fixed age-defined population. Apuntes 60 describes students in operating programme establishments across preschool, primary and secondary education, including youth and adult education; the selected autism tables do not provide an age-specific denominator. For 2019–2023, we added its historical autism and autism spectrum disorder (ASD)–Asperger categories and divided by all PIE students in the same table when describing programme composition. The report from the National Higher Education Quality Assurance System (SINACES) supplied subsequent autism totals and a distinct series for autism special schools. Its programme-applicant counts were kept separate from enrolment denominators. We retained the source transition and the five-student 2022 discrepancy explicitly, allowing readers to distinguish changes in recorded categories from harmonisation choices.<sup>10,11</sup>

The National Board of School Assistance and Scholarships (JUNAEB) school survey was examined but is not used for any estimate in this article. Its expansion weights do not supply the school-cluster and stratum information required for design-based inference; the 2023–24 autism variables contain positive selections and blanks rather than explicit negative responses, whereas 2025 adds explicit 0/1 values conditional on a medical-diagnosis filter, so a valid yes/no filter is not necessarily a complete autism outcome; and the 2024 grade-9 autism item is entirely empty and is therefore not estimable rather than zero. No JUNAEB figure, weighted interval or numerical claim appears in this article.
A10. Screening and assisted referral by era

Screening and assisted referral were retained as supplementary context because their discontinuities show why a single continuous screening series would be misleading. In 2019–22, A03 (REM assessment-scale module) records Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT) tests performed or altered among children already identified with language or social-area alteration. The 2023–24 Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised with Follow-Up (M-CHAT-R/F) categories are displayed separately, with first-part risk classifications and a second-part referral item. The additional 2024 indicators address ages 31–59 months. The 2025 redesign identifies M-CHAT-R/F results in ages 16–30 months and suspected autism at 30–59 months, retaining the published age boundary rather than harmonising it to the previous era. A27 (REM health-education module) assisted referrals are a separate annual count. Counts sum observed monthly values and report the number of establishments with a source record during that year; this is not evidence of complete reporting in every month at each establishment. All selected national series have records from 12 distinct months, including 2025, but network completeness is unknown. Missing items are not interpreted as zero. Repeated exact records have a small effect in selected A03 2024 counts (one low-risk record and four evaluations aged 31–59 months); the primary file totals and the deduplication sensitivity are retained. Independently aggregated items are not assumed to be nested person-level stages, and no conversion or referral-completion probability is calculated.<sup>2</sup>
A11. Territorial methods and ecological comparisons

Territorial analyses used a fixed 346-commune Unique Territorial Code (CUT) crosswalk and INE resident population projections with a 2017 census base. GRD numerators locate episodes by reported residence; REM numerators locate activity at the reporting establishment. Therefore, REM divided by commune residents describes the spatial distribution of reported services relative to population and is not a risk estimate for those residents. The existing crosswalk harmonised commune codes and name aliases; all selected REM rows linked to it. Boundaries were kept fixed across years, with Ñuble represented consistently as region 16. No new boundary reconstruction was undertaken. Two GRD episodes with unknown residence were excluded from territorial numerators. A missing GRD residence–year row denotes no recorded eligible episode in the observed network, not complete ascertainment of autism among residents.

GRD spatial maps retained the 2019–2024 window. For commune c, E<sub>c</sub>=Σ<sub>tas</sub> N<sub>ctas</sub> r<sub>tas</sub>, where N is the resident population and r the national GRD episode rate for year t, age group a and sex s. Expected counts were multiplied by a common factor so that their total equalled the geocoded observed total; SIR<sub>c</sub>=O<sub>c</sub>/E<sub>c</sub>. Unknown-age/sex episodes remain in the observed numerator, so this calibration does not restore their missing covariates. Marshall empirical-Bayes smoothing shrank SIR<sub>c</sub> towards the overall ratio μ with weight w<sub>c</sub>=E<sub>c</sub>/(E<sub>c</sub>+μ/τ²), using the non-negative method-of-moments between-commune variance τ². Smoothed ratios are (w<sub>c</sub> SIR<sub>c</sub>)+(1−w<sub>c</sub>)μ; when τ²=0, all valid ratios shrink to μ. Crude commune ratios and alternative neighbourhood weights were retained as sensitivity analyses. Regional endpoint comparisons in Figure S6c are crude recorded episodes per 100 000 residents, with exact Poisson intervals; they are not age-standardised or estimates of uncertainty in network ascertainment.<sup>12</sup> Here, SIR denotes the indirectly standardised recorded-episode ratio, observed divided by expected episodes.

The spatial graph comprised 342 communes, preserving the existing continental restriction that excluded Juan Fernández (05104), Isla de Pascua (05201), Cabo de Hornos (12201) and Antártica (12202); only Cabo de Hornos retained geometry inside the displayed map extent. Polygon topology was retained when constructing queen contiguity; weights were standardised by row. Four islands in this graph (CUT 01404, 10206, 11203 and 12303) were attached to their nearest neighbour. Alternatives used four and eight nearest neighbours or inverse centroid distance, with a 142·31-km threshold ensuring at least one neighbour. Distances and map areas used a Chile-centred Albers equal-area projection. Global Moran I and local Moran statistics used the existing 999 permutations and seed 20260905; the local pseudo-p values were checked against the Benjamini–Hochberg threshold q=0·05 across 342 communes. A non-rejection is not evidence of spatial homogeneity. Maps preserve the original three geographic bands at the same metric scale; these layout bands do not define analytical macrozones.<sup>13–15</sup>

The Gini coefficient orders communes by their recorded-episode-to-resident ratio. Let X<sub>j</sub> and Y<sub>j</sub> be cumulative shares of resident population and recorded episodes after this ordering. G=1−Σ<sub>j</sub>(X<sub>j</sub>−X<sub>j−1</sub>)(Y<sub>j</sub>+Y<sub>j−1</sub>). Thus population weights, rather than equal commune weights, determine the Lorenz curve. All 346 communes, including true zero recorded counts, contribute. The same Gini calculation was repeated using the fixed 65-hospital GRD panel as a coverage sensitivity. Annual coverage is separately defined as the number with at least one recorded episode. Neither a smaller Gini nor a larger count of positive communes establishes equity or complete coverage.

The corrected cross-source analysis used 2021–2024 for all three indicators. A05 included only strict-autism entry code 05990022; P2 included P2500500 in December, covering ages 0–19 throughout this common window; the 2019–2020 age 0–9 era was not mixed into these correlations. Valid numeric rows, including zero, contributed; empty cells and absent rows did not become zero. A commune entered a pairwise analysis only if the relevant REM indicator had at least one valid establishment value in each of the four years. This rule establishes annual value presence, not monthly completeness or reporting by every establishment. One A05 row in 2024 had an empty total and was excluded; there were four reported-zero A05 rows across the window. Selected P2 December rows contained no reported zeros or empty totals. No selected exact duplicate or conflicting key was found. The stable-establishment sensitivity required a valid value from the same establishment in every common-window year; it likewise does not establish monthly completeness.

For flows, the window indicator was 100 000×Σ<sub>t</sub> O<sub>ct</sub>/Σ<sub>t</sub> N<sub>ct</sub>. P2 was explicitly the mean of the four December stocks for ages 0–19 divided by the mean of the four all-age resident populations, multiplied by 100 000. Algebraically this equals the ratio of sums, but the stock numerator is not interpreted as cumulative unique people. Spearman coefficients used unweighted territorial ranks with tied values averaged. Pair-specific complete commune sets were aggregated before computing regional coefficients, preserving a like-for-like geographical subset at the two scales. All three source pairs were retained. Limited sensitivities used a common three-source set, stable establishments, exclusion of positive counts of 1–4, exclusion of Metropolitana, raw standardised ratios, empirical Bayes (EB) ratios, counts without denominators and population-rank adjustment. A05 standardisation used the strict-autism national age–sex schedule; P2 had population-size standardisation only. Population-rank adjustment correlated residuals from separate regressions of each indicator rank on an intercept and the rank of mean population; it remained descriptive.

Ordinary Spearman p-values and Fisher-z intervals assume dependence structures not justified here. Independent resampling of communes would not resolve spatial dependence. A spatial block or spatial-surrogate analysis would require a justified block scale or null spatial model and sufficient independent units; these were not established in this bounded correction. Coefficients are therefore presented descriptively, without confidence intervals or significance stars. Bivariate Moran addresses association with neighbours and does not replace uncertainty for a same-commune Spearman coefficient; it was not used to infer referral or individual concordance. No externally justified pre-existing macrozone classification was identified, so a fourth within-macrozone correlation panel was omitted. This decision preserved the three specified source pairs without constructing zones from their observed association.

The dated original plan specified spatial false-discovery control if territorial analyses were included, but did not contain the detailed spatial specifications later stated in the implementation header. Existing GRD spatial analyses are retained as secondary exploratory analyses. Local cells with 1–4 positive episodes are hatched or omitted from scatter displays; their EB values and identifying labels are not displayed. True zero is shown separately. Correlation coefficients retain eligible low-count communes, with exclusion of such cells as a sensitivity.
Territorial displays suppress cells below five records; suppressed values and their ranks are not reported, and no display allows their reconstruction.
